title: {{NAME}} and the Clockwork Garden of Starlight
moral: Wonder and logic need each other to see the world whole.

pages.content: The Clockwork Garden existed in the space between two heartbeats of the old grandfather clock in {{NAME}}'s hallway. He had discovered this quite by accident when he was trying to fix the clock's missing pendulum weight with a bent spoon. The garden spread out before him now like a dream someone had taken great care to build: rows of mechanical flowers that opened and closed in perfect rhythm, hedgerows trimmed into the shapes of impossible animals, and pathways of glowing amber glass that chimed softly underfoot. At the garden's heart stood a fountain, and drinking from the fountain was a unicorn made of no material {{NAME}} had ever seen, part silver, part starlight, part something that was simply beautiful and refused to be named. Around the unicorn's hooves, small animals moved: clockwork rabbits with sapphire eyes, a copper sparrow that sang a single looping note, and a tortoise whose shell was a working orrery of tiny spinning planets. {{NAME}} stood at the garden gate and forgot entirely about the bent spoon.

pages.content: The unicorn raised her head and regarded {{NAME}} with eyes that held entire galaxies in them, swirling and patient. 'You are the one who bent the spoon,' she said. Her voice was like music played on an instrument not yet invented. 'I am NOVA,' said a different voice, and {{NAME}} turned to find a robot sitting cross-legged in the roots of a clockwork oak, its body slim and polished silver, its head a perfect sphere fitted with a single large eye of pale blue light. It had a notebook and was sketching the mechanical flowers with extraordinary precision. 'I catalogue this garden,' NOVA said. 'I measure and record every mechanism.' It looked at the unicorn, then back at {{NAME}}. 'I have measured every flower here but I cannot explain why they are beautiful. My equations describe the geometry but not the feeling.' The unicorn's galaxy eyes turned to NOVA with something that looked very like fondness. 'That,' she said, 'is the only honest thing you have said in three hundred years, NOVA.' The robot's blue eye flickered. It looked, {{NAME}} thought, almost flustered.

pages.content: The problem arrived without knocking, as problems often do. A section of the garden's central mechanism, the great brass heart buried beneath the fountain that kept all the clockwork animals alive, had begun to wind down. The copper sparrow had stopped singing. Two of the sapphire-eyed rabbits sat perfectly still, like elegant but useless paperweights. The tortoise's planets had frozen mid-orbit. NOVA was already at the fountain base, its blue eye scanning. 'The winding key is broken,' it said. 'I can see exactly which component has failed. But the key slot requires a very specific shape. I do not have the tool.' {{NAME}} thought of the bent spoon still in his pocket. He pulled it out. NOVA stared at it. 'That is a spoon,' it said. 'Bent,' {{NAME}} agreed. 'Bent at precisely the angle of the key slot, if I'm not mistaken.' NOVA scanned the spoon with its blue eye, and the light flickered rapidly, almost like excitement. 'You are not mistaken,' it said, quietly. The unicorn stepped forward, lowered her horn to the spoon, and where her horn touched, the metal straightened and sharpened into a perfect key. Together, {{NAME}} and NOVA fitted it into the lock and turned.

pages.content: The brass heart beneath the garden gave one enormous, sonorous clunk, and then began to beat again. The wave of returning life moved outward from the fountain like a warm ripple across still water. The sapphire rabbits blinked, twitched their ears, and began to nibble the amber pathway. The tortoise's planets resumed their slow orbits, even more precise than before. And the copper sparrow, perched on NOVA's sphere-head, opened its beak and sang. The note it produced was not single this time but a whole sweeping melody, as though the pause had filled it with a song it had been saving. {{NAME}} felt the music move through him in a way he had no words for. He looked at NOVA. The robot's blue eye was very still. 'Is that what beauty feels like?' it asked, very quietly. 'I think so,' said {{NAME}}. NOVA was silent for a long moment, recording something carefully in its notebook. The unicorn pressed her starlight cheek gently against the robot's silver sphere, and NOVA made a sound that no one had ever heard a robot make before. Something between a hum and a sigh.

pages.content: The clockwork garden slowed toward evening, the mechanical flowers folding gently, the amber pathways dimming to a warm rose-gold. The copper sparrow nestled into {{NAME}}'s teal jacket pocket, its small wings still trembling faintly with song. NOVA sat back against the clockwork oak and opened its notebook to a fresh page, on which it began to draw {{NAME}} from memory, capturing every detail of his face and the way he had looked while listening to the sparrow. The unicorn lay down beside the fountain, her starlight coat softening to a gentle glow like a lamp turned low. 'Come back tomorrow,' she said, in her music-instrument voice. 'There are three hundred and forty-seven other mechanisms I have not shown you yet.' {{NAME}} felt the world beyond the clock begin to pull him gently back. He tucked the memory of the sparrow's song somewhere safe inside his chest and stepped toward the gate. He was almost through when NOVA called after him. 'I recorded the feeling of the song,' it said. 'I am not sure what to label the file.' {{NAME}} smiled back. 'Try wonder,' he said.
